claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle failure.
Localized dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause stress concentrations and brittle failure in the untreated alloy.
A controlled heat treatment will promote solute redistribution at internal boundaries.
The heat treatment will produce microstructural refinement at the internal boundaries.
The modified internal boundaries will have a reduced propensity for dislocation pile-ups.
Solute redistribution at lamellar-colony interfaces will transform the interfaces into more compliant zones.
More compliant interfaces will reduce local stress concentrations during deformation.
Reducing local stress concentrations will suppress microcracking during deformation.
The controlled heat treatment will increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The controlled heat treatment will maintain or slightly improve tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The controlled heat treatment will delay crack initiation and propagation.
Overly aggressive heat treatments could cause phase coarsening or undesirable precipitate formation.
The proposed mechanism may involve trace microalloying elements that are naturally present or added in low amounts.
The response should be evaluated by room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing at moderate strain rates.

contradictions.description: The stated single intervention is heat treatment, but the mechanism also allows trace microalloying elements to be added. Such an addition would be a separate compositional intervention rather than heat treatment alone.
